title: When there is no inverse
objectives: Recognise a singular matrix by the way it squashes the plane.

screens.prose: The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ k & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ moves the dashed unit square to the shaded shape. Its sides are the columns: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_1 = (2, k)$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2 = (1, 1)$.

derive.caption: $k$ = {{k}}: $ad - bc = 2 - k$ = {{fixed(2 - k, 2)}}, shaded area = {{fixed(abs(2 - k), 2)}}

screens.question: Slide $k$ until the square is squashed flat.

hints.text: Watch the shaded area in the caption as you slide.
The shape is flat when its two sides point along the same line.
The side (1, 1) has slope 1. The side $(2, k)$ has slope 1 when $k = 2$.

feedback.correct: At $k = 2$ the shape is a segment with no area.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep sliding until the shaded area reads 0.

byKey.flipped: Past $k = 2$ the shape has opened up again, mirror-imaged. Slide back until it is flat.

explain.text: At $k = 2$ the columns (2, 2) and (1, 1) point the same way. The square flattens into a segment with zero area. Every point of the plane lands on one line.

screens.prose: Slide $k$ through its whole range. The caption tracks $ad - bc$ and the shaded area side by side.

derive.caption: $k$ = {{k}}: $ad - bc = 2 - k$ = {{fixed(2 - k, 2)}}, shaded area = {{fixed(abs(2 - k), 2)}}

screens.question: How is the shaded area related to $ad - bc$?

options.why: At $k = 3$, $ad - bc = -1$ but the shape has area 1. An area is never negative.
Here $ad = 2$ for every $k$, yet the area changes as you slide.
At $k = 1$ that gives $2 + 1 = 3$, but the area is 1. The $bc$ part is subtracted.

feedback.correct: The area is the size of $ad - bc$, ignoring its sign.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two numbers in the caption at $k = 0$, $1$ and $3$.

byKey.signed: At $k = 3$, $ad - bc = -1$ but the shape has area 1. An area is never negative.
byKey.ad: Here $ad = 2$ for every $k$, yet the area changes as you slide.
byKey.plus: At $k = 1$ that gives $2 + 1 = 3$, but the area is 1. The $bc$ part is subtracted.

explain.text: The area is $|2 - k|$ for every $k$: the size of $ad - bc$. That number is the **determinant**, $\det\mathbf{A}$. It is the factor by which $\mathbf{A}$ scales every area.

screens.prose: At $k = 3$, $\det\mathbf{A} = 2 - 3 = -1$, yet the shape has area 1. In the unit square, $\mathbf{e}_2$ is a quarter turn anticlockwise from $\mathbf{e}_1$.

derive.caption: $k$ = {{k}}: $ad - bc = 2 - k$ = {{fixed(2 - k, 2)}}, shaded area = {{fixed(abs(2 - k), 2)}}

screens.question: What does the minus sign record?

options.text: The plane is flipped: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2$ now sits clockwise from $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_1$

options.why: It sits above the axis at $k = 3$. The sign records an order, not a position.
The area is 1, the same as the unit square.
Only a zero determinant does that. This shape still has area 1, so nothing collapsed.

hints.text: Go from $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_1$ to $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2$ the short way round. Clockwise or anticlockwise?
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_1 = (2, 3)$ is steeper than $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2 = (1, 1)$.
From the steeper side to the shallower one is clockwise: the opposite of $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $\mathbf{e}_2$.

feedback.correct: A negative determinant flips the plane over, like a mirror.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the turn from $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $\mathbf{e}_2$ with the turn from their images.

byKey.below: It sits above the axis at $k = 3$. The sign records an order, not a position.
byKey.shrank: The area is 1, the same as the unit square.
byKey.no-inverse: Only a zero determinant does that. This shape still has area 1, so nothing collapsed.

explain.text: $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $\mathbf{e}_2$ turns anticlockwise, but $(2, 3)$ to $(1, 1)$ turns clockwise. The matrix has flipped the plane over. The sign of $\det\mathbf{A}$ records orientation; its size records area.

screens.prose: A new matrix: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Its columns (1, 2) and (3, 1) are the sides of the shaded image.
screens.question: What is the area of the shaded image?

hints.text: Compute $ad - bc$ first.
$ad - bc = 1 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 2$.
$\det\mathbf{A} = -5$. The area is its size.

feedback.correct: $|1 - 6| = 5$ square units, and the image is flipped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $ad - bc$, then take its size.

byKey.negative: That is the determinant. An area is its size, 5; the minus says the image is flipped.

explain.text: $\det\mathbf{A} = 1 - 6 = -5$. The image has 5 times the area of the unit square. The minus sign says it is a mirror image.

screens.prose: The system $x + 3y = 6$ and $2x + 6y = 6$ has $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det\mathbf{A} = 6 - 6 = 0$. Here are its two lines.
screens.question: How many solutions does the system have?

options.why: You expected a crossing, but the lines have the same slope, $-\tfrac{1}{3}$. Parallel lines never meet.
That needs the same line. Doubling the first equation gives $2x + 6y = 12$, not 6.

hints.text: A solution is a point on both lines.
Both lines have slope $-\tfrac{1}{3}$.
Same slope, different heights: the lines are parallel and never cross.

feedback.correct: Parallel lines share no point, so there is no solution.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a point on both lines.

byKey.one: You expected a crossing, but the lines have the same slope, $-\tfrac{1}{3}$. Parallel lines never meet.
byKey.many: That needs the same line. Doubling the first equation gives $2x + 6y = 12$, not 6.

explain.text: Row 2 of $\mathbf{A}$ is twice row 1, so both lines have slope $-\tfrac{1}{3}$. Twice the first equation says $2x + 6y = 12$, but the second says 6. No point can satisfy both.

screens.prose: Same $\mathbf{A}$, new right-hand side: $x + 3y = 6$ and $2x + 6y = 12$. Only $\mathbf{b}$ changed.
screens.question: How many solutions does the system have now?

options.why: Same slope, but now the same height too: the second line lies on top of the first.
There is no single crossing: the two lines coincide, so they share every point.

hints.text: Divide the second equation by 2.
$2x + 6y = 12$ halves to $x + 3y = 6$: the first equation again.
Both equations describe one line, so every point on it works: (6, 0), (0, 2), (3, 1) and so on.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the second equation with twice the first.

byKey.none: Same slope, but now the same height too: the second line lies on top of the first.
byKey.one: There is no single crossing: the two lines coincide, so they share every point.

explain.text: The second equation is twice the first, so the lines coincide. Every point on $x + 3y = 6$ solves the system. With $\det\mathbf{A} = 0$, $\mathbf{b}$ decides between no solution and infinitely many, but never exactly one.

screens.prose: A colleague says a matrix with no zero entries always has an inverse. Test the claim on the matrix below.
screens.question: Does $\mathbf{A}$ have an inverse?

options.why: No zero entry does not guarantee an inverse. Here column 2 is twice column 1, so the plane still collapses.
You added $bc$: $4 + 4 = 8$. The determinant subtracts, $4 - 4 = 0$.
Repeated entries do not matter. $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ repeats entries and has $\det = 3$.

hints.text: Compute $ad - bc$.
$ad = 1 \cdot 4$ and $bc = 2 \cdot 2$.
$ad - bc = 4 - 4 = 0$. Column 2, (2, 4), is twice column 1, (1, 2).

feedback.correct: $\det\mathbf{A} = 0$, so there is no inverse, zeros or not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide with the determinant, not with the entries one by one.

byKey.no-zero: No zero entry does not guarantee an inverse. Here column 2 is twice column 1, so the plane still collapses.
byKey.repeat: Repeated entries do not matter. $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ repeats entries and has $\det = 3$.

explain.text: $\det\mathbf{A} = 1 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2 = 0$. Column 2 is twice column 1, so both columns lie on one line and the plane collapses onto it. What matters is dependence between the columns, not zeros.

screens.prose: You saw $\det\mathbf{A} = ad - bc$ scale every area by $|\det\mathbf{A}|$, its sign recording a flip. When $\det\mathbf{A} = 0$ the plane collapses onto a line. Different points land on one spot, so nothing can undo it. Such a matrix is **singular**: $$\det\mathbf{A} = 0 \iff \mathbf{A}^{-1} \text{ does not exist}$$
screens.question: For which $k$ is $\begin{pmatrix} k & 6 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ singular?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $ad - bc = 3k - 12$ equal to 0.

explain.text: $\det = 3k - 6 \cdot 2 = 3k - 12$, which is 0 at $k = 4$. Then column 1 is $(4, 2)$ and column 2 is $(6, 3)$, both multiples of $(2, 1)$.

screens.prose: Why does a zero determinant go with parallel columns? Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ with columns $(a, c)$ and $(b, d)$, and suppose they lie on one line.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Column 2 is $t$ times column 1: $b = ta$ and $d = tc$, the columns are parallel
$= tac - tac$, multiply out each product
$= 0$, so parallel columns force a zero determinant

hints.text: Start from the assumption about the columns.
Substitute $b = ta$ and $d = tc$ into $ad - bc$.
Assume, substitute, multiply out, cancel.

feedback.correct: The two products are equal, so they cancel.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with what parallel columns mean, then substitute.

byKey.l2: You cannot substitute before saying what $b$ and $d$ are. Start with the assumption.

explain.text: Parallel columns make $ad$ and $bc$ the same product, $tac$, so they cancel. The converse holds too: $ad - bc = 0$ forces the columns onto one line. That is why the square collapsed.

screens.prose: The desk swaps option Q for option S. S's greeks are exactly 1.2 times P's. The target is still delta 200 and vega £150.
screens.question: What can the desk do with P and S alone?

options.text: No mix hits it: every mix has vega equal to 0.4 times its delta

options.why: $\det\mathbf{A} = 0.50 \cdot 0.24 - 0.60 \cdot 0.20 = 0$, so there is no inverse to use.

options.text: Buy 400 of P and none of S
options.why: 400 of P gives delta 200 but vega only 80, not 150.

options.text: Many mixes hit it, so pick the cheapest
options.why: Many mixes hit targets with vega $= 0.4 \times$ delta, such as (200, 80). The target (200, 150) is off that line.

hints.text: Compute $\det\mathbf{A}$ with the two options as columns.
Each option has vega $= 0.4 \times$ delta, so any mix does too. The target needs $150 = 0.4 \times 200 = 80$.

feedback.correct: Proportional greeks span only one line of targets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare vega to delta for each option, and for the target.

byKey.inverse: $\det\mathbf{A} = 0.50 \cdot 0.24 - 0.60 \cdot 0.20 = 0$, so there is no inverse to use.
byKey.only-p: 400 of P gives delta 200 but vega only 80, not 150.
byKey.many: Many mixes hit targets with vega $= 0.4 \times$ delta, such as (200, 80). The target (200, 150) is off that line.

explain.text: Both columns are multiples of $(1, 0.4)$, so every mix has vega $= 0.4 \times$ delta. The target $(200, 150)$ is off that line: no solution. The desk needs an option with a different vega-to-delta ratio.

screens.prose: A company has two share classes. Each has 25% volatility and their returns are perfectly correlated, so $$\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.0625 & 0.0625 \\ 0.0625 & 0.0625 \end{pmatrix}$$ The minimum-variance weights are usually proportional to $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}$.
screens.question: What happens when you look for the minimum-variance mix?

options.text: Every fully invested mix has the same variance, so the minimum is not unique
The 50/50 mix has the lowest variance
options.why: With correlation 1 there is no diversification. A 50/50 mix has variance 0.0625, the same as 100% in one class.
$\det\Sigma = 0.0625^2 - 0.0625^2 = 0$, so $\Sigma$ has no inverse.
That needs a mix that cancels out. With weights summing to 1, the variance is $0.0625(w_1 + w_2)^2 = 0.0625$.

hints.text: Compute $\det\Sigma$.
The two columns of $\Sigma$ are identical, so $\det\Sigma = 0$.
A mix $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ has variance $\mathbf{w}^T\Sigma\mathbf{w} = 0.0625(w_1 + w_2)^2 = 0.0625$ whatever the split.

feedback.correct: Every fully invested split has variance 0.0625: no unique minimum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\det\Sigma$, then the variance of a general mix.

byKey.half: With correlation 1 there is no diversification. A 50/50 mix has variance 0.0625, the same as 100% in one class.
byKey.zero: That needs a mix that cancels out. With weights summing to 1, the variance is $0.0625(w_1 + w_2)^2 = 0.0625$.

explain.text: $\det\Sigma = 0$, so $\Sigma$ is singular and $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}$ does not exist. Every split of the money has variance 0.0625, so infinitely many mixes tie. A singular covariance matrix means two assets carry the same risk.

ideas: $\det\mathbf{A} = ad - bc$ scales every area by $|\det\mathbf{A}|$; a negative sign means the plane is flipped.
When $\det\mathbf{A} = 0$ the columns are parallel and the plane collapses onto a line, so nothing can undo it.
A singular system has no solution or infinitely many, depending on $\mathbf{b}$, never exactly one.

formula.name: Determinant
formula.tex: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc
